original_question: For isotropic two-phase composites with complex effective permittivity, some known geometries place the effective permittivity on a particular bounding circular arc in the complex plane and can therefore attain maximal absorption in the quasistatic limit. Are there other microgeometries with isotropic effective permittivities whose effective responses also lie on that same arc?
target_in_paper: Problem 3.4 in §3: "Are there other geometries with isotropic effective permittivities that lie on the arc?" ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the core existence question, the focus on isotropic effective complex permittivity, the fact that the relevant responses lie on a bounding circular arc in the complex plane, and the motivation from achieving maximal absorption in the quasistatic regime. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
missing_details: The paper is not asking this in arbitrary dimension: the immediate setup is the three-dimensional isotropic case discussed just before Problem 3.4. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

The constituent materials are themselves two isotropic phases, mixed in fixed proportions; that hypothesis is part of the bounding-arc discussion leading into Problem 3.4. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

The paper works with the effective complex electrical permittivity, and explicitly notes the equivalent conductivity-language formulation (and equivalently magnetic permeability) in the quasistatic reduction. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

To be stand-alone, "isotropic effective permittivity" should be read as a scalar effective response (the isotropic effective tensor is a scalar multiple of the identity, written earlier in §3 in conductivity notation as σ*(σ)I). ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

The relevant arc is not just any bounding arc: it is the previously known second bounding circular arc, the one corresponding to conductivity functions σ*(σ) having a single pole at a finite negative real value of σ. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

The nearby context specifies the known examples more concretely: first five microgeometries were known to give five points on that arc, and then three additional multiple-rank laminate geometries were found on the same arc. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

The maximal-absorption statement is conditional: the paper says that geometries on that arc can have the maximum possible absorption depending on the material moduli, rather than unconditionally for every choice of phases. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

If you want the quasistatic hypothesis stated explicitly, the paper defines it as the regime in which the wavelengths and attenuation lengths in each phase are much larger than the microstructure; later on the same page it is paraphrased as wavelength much larger than the unit-cell size. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
refined_question: In the three-dimensional quasistatic setting of §3, for composites made from two isotropic phases mixed in fixed proportions and having an isotropic effective complex electrical permittivity (equivalently, scalar effective complex conductivity), are there microgeometries beyond the five previously identified examples and the three additional multiple-rank laminate geometries whose effective response lies on the previously known second bounding circular arc of the admissible lens-shaped region in the complex plane—that is, the arc corresponding to conductivity functions σ*(σ) with exactly one pole at a finite negative real value of σ—and which therefore, for suitable material moduli, can realize the maximum possible absorption? ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalent conductivity-language formulation: For three-dimensional isotropic composites of two isotropic phases, are there additional microgeometries whose scalar effective conductivity function σ*(σ) lies on the previously known second bounding circular arc, the arc associated with conductivity functions having one pole at a finite negative real value of σ? ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
justification: The draft is aiming at Problem 3.4, not the broader characterization problems 3.1–3.3 and not the neighboring simplification question 3.5, because it asks exactly whether there are further geometries whose isotropic effective responses lie on the same special arc associated with maximal absorption. The refined version only makes explicit the hypotheses and identifications that are implicit in the surrounding paragraph: three-dimensional isotropic composites, two isotropic phases in fixed proportions, the quasistatic conductivity/electrical-permittivity equivalence, and the fact that "the arc" means the previously known second bounding arc characterized by a one-pole conductivity function. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
